solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Country hat off before sex with one

indicators.note: something that has gone off is spoilt or out of order, so the word before it is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
IT is a long-standing slang term for sex appeal or sex
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A sex tourist doffs his hat on arriving abroad and pairs off with someone.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex is a crossword staple; Tahiti is loosely called a country though it belongs to French Polynesia.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahiti is a Pacific island nation-like territory, treated here as an example of a country.

clue.text: One preferred by those who wait to welcome Latin piss-artist

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.clueFragment: One preferred by those who wait
blocks.note: waiters favour a customer who leaves a generous gratuity
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: Waiting staff warmly greet a Latin drunk who is a favourite customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those who wait' are waiters, and the one they prefer is the customer who leaves money on the table. Piss-artist is British slang for a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: A tippler is a habitual drinker, and a piss-artist is British slang for a drunkard.

clue.text: Pathetic cry: "Physio can't if unpunctuated!"

definitions.note: the definition is CANT once the apostrophe is removed

indicators.note: pathetic means feeble or a mess, so the letters it governs are in a sorry jumble

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient whines that the physiotherapist says they cannot do something.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip the apostrophe from 'can't' and it becomes cant, meaning insincere pious talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Cant is sanctimonious, insincere talk, which is a synonym for hypocrisy.

clue.text: Nick to perpetrate this article by newspaper

definitions.note: to nick is to commit this act

blocks.note: the definite article
the Financial Times, a London newspaper

explanation.surface: A tabloid reporter steals a story, with a jab at newspaper ethics.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a little sentence: to nick something is to carry out this crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicking is British slang for stealing, and the act it performs is a theft.

clue.text: Try to get rid of a lot of effort grabbing inside of bum

definitions.text: Try to get rid of a lot

indicators.note: the inside of a short word is its central letter, so only that one is kept
grabbing something means clutching it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: effort or activity
the middle letter of bum

explanation.surface: Someone grabs a backside with a great deal of effort while trying to shake them off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot' looks like 'a great deal', but it is a lot in a saleroom; the definition ends at 'lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: To auction goods is to offer them for sale, each item being a lot under the hammer.

clue.text: "Pissed", "canned" – ugh, it's all the same

indicators.note: pissed means drunk, so the letters that follow stagger into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A weary drinker notes that 'pissed' and 'canned' are the same thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Both quoted words mean drunk, which fits the surface; only the second is fodder, the first telling you to mix it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unchanged stays exactly as it was, so it is all the same as before.

clue.text: Allure of top extremist Tory leaders pressing Cameron's U-turn

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so each word gives its opening letter
a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters run backwards
pressing means squeezing around something, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: the first letters of these three words
David Cameron was the Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Leading right-wingers lure the Prime Minister into a policy reversal.
explanation.walkthrough: Cameron was Prime Minister, abbreviated PM; it turns round and sits inside the three initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To allure someone is to entice or attract them, a synonym of tempt.

clue.text: see 9dn.
Cope with lap dancing with jerk beside oneself

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and land in new places

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a tic is an involuntary twitch or jerk

explanation.surface: A man struggles to cope at a lap-dancing club, next to some jerk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult for a person, but it is a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Apoplectic means overcome with fury, the idiom being beside oneself with rage.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) e.g. "Bloody platitudes reveal sod all that's new"

definitions.text: e.g. "Bloody platitudes reveal sod all that's new"

blocks.clueFragment: e.g. "Bloody platitudes reveal sod all that's new"
blocks.note: surface: a grumble about clichés that tell you nothing
setter's reading: the swear-word becomes its British synonym, and platitudes are statements so plain everyone knows them

explanation.surface: A critic swears at hackneyed sayings that reveal nothing fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: Bleeding is a British euphemism for bloody, and the whole quotation is an example of stating the bleeding obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: Platitudes that tell you nothing new are, in British idiom, stating something blindingly plain to everyone.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) Advance at an end: thus Brian's demand of Brenda?

blocks.note: to advance is to move forward
something at an end is over

explanation.surface: A note on Prince Charles impatiently waiting for his mother to give up the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda and Prince Charles Brian; the heir's demand is that she stand aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking someone to make way or stand aside for you is an informal command to give up place.

clue.text: Formal habit of jailed publisher associated with fix

blocks.note: Conrad Black, newspaper proprietor jailed for fraud
to fix or fasten

explanation.surface: A disgraced press baron is dressed up and linked to a rigged deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Conrad Black owned the Daily Telegraph and served prison time in the US for fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: Black tie is the dress code for formal evening wear, a habit in the sense of clothing.

clue.text: Just after gold – god, that could be Archer, to stretch a point?

definitions.text: that could be Archer, to stretch a point?

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: A sneer at Jeffrey Archer chasing money and posing as a literary god.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer is a bestselling novelist and convicted perjurer; calling him a writer 'stretches a point' is Private Eye's jibe.
explanation.definitionFit: Archer writes novels, so he is an example of a writer, if only grudgingly allowed.

clue.text: Leaderless party members securing good binges

indicators.note: without a leader means the front letter is dropped
securing something means holding it fast inside

blocks.note: members of the Conservative Party
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Rank-and-file Tories without a leader enjoy some fine drinking sessions.
explanation.walkthrough: Tories are members of Britain's Conservative Party; lose the first letter, then tuck in the G.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy is a bout of wild excess, so binges of indulgence is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Scored high but made a complete balls of it

definitions.text: made a complete balls of it

blocks.note: to score is slang for having sex, as is to screw
high, raised up

explanation.surface: Someone gets a high mark yet still somehow botches the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scored high' looks like a good result, but scored is sexual slang; to make a balls of something is British slang for bungling it.
explanation.definitionFit: To screw up is to bungle, the same as making a complete mess or balls of something.

clue.text: Incapable when member reduced in size

blocks.note: a limb, a member of the body
smaller in amount

explanation.surface: Someone becomes unable to cope after losing a limb.
explanation.walkthrough: Legless is British slang for very drunk, and incapable is the police-report sense of drunk and incapable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being legless means too drunk to stand, as in the British charge drunk and incapable.

clue.text: Perpetuate a stitch-up and rather exaggerate the fact

blocks.note: first meaning: to do decorative needlework, a literal stitching
second meaning: to add fanciful detail to a story

explanation.surface: A frame-up is kept going by someone who overstates the evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: A stitch-up is British slang for a frame-up, but here it is taken literally as needlework.
explanation.definitionFit: Embroidering decorates cloth with stitches, and figuratively embellishes a tale beyond the truth.

clue.text: Evergreen Tory extremely contrary with a beer swilling exterior

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters
contrary means going the opposite way, so the pair is read backwards
swilling sloshes liquid about, so these letters are churned into a new order
an exterior is the outside, so these letters wrap around the rest

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Tory
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A perennially awkward Tory contrarian is surrounded by beer-swilling drinkers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evergreen Tory' reads as a long-serving MP, but evergreen is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The bay tree is a laurel that keeps its leaves all year, an example of an evergreen.

clue.text: State gets one through? Throw up first

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: to lob is to throw
the Roman numeral for one
via means by way of, through

explanation.surface: A nation pulls through, after first being sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw up' looks like vomiting, but it is a throw read upwards in this down clue, and 'first' puts it at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolivia is a South American country, an example of a sovereign state.

clue.text: Balls twisted when going to bed? Explode

indicators.note: twisted round means turned to face the other way, so the name is read backwards

blocks.note: Ed Balls, the Labour politician, supplies his first name
a bunk is a bed

explanation.surface: A crude picture of genitals twisting at bedtime before an outburst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is not a body part or nonsense here but Ed Balls, Labour shadow chancellor, whose first name turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: To explode a myth is to expose it as false, which is what debunking does.

clue.text: No need for press's inaccurate description of Lady Thatcher?

blocks.note: first meaning: fabric that does not need pressing
second meaning: denying that she was the Iron Lady, which would be wrong

explanation.surface: The press hardly needs to describe Margaret Thatcher wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' suggests newspapers, but it is pressing clothes. Thatcher's famous nickname was the Iron Lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-iron fabric needs no pressing, and the phrase would contradict Thatcher's Iron Lady nickname.

clue.text: Past saying "Shot loads, wife"

indicators.note: something shot is wrecked or worn out, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A smutty remark overheard about a husband, a wife and their past.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks dress the wordplay as something said, but only the last two words are fodder and abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An old saw is a long-established proverb, a saying from the past.

clue.text: Drugs tipped onto booze which provides immunity

indicators.note: tipped over means upended, so in a down clue the letters run bottom to top

blocks.note: Es are ecstasy tablets
rum is an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Pills knocked back with alcohol, as if they offered protection.
explanation.walkthrough: E is the usual crossword shorthand for ecstasy, so drugs in the plural is Es.
explanation.definitionFit: A serum contains antibodies taken from blood and is given to provide immunity against disease.

clue.text: A French incursion into bodice-ripping: Frigidly Inaccessible

indicators.note: ripping tears the garment apart, so its letters are scattered and reassembled
an incursion goes inside territory, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
un is French for a

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's romantic advance on a bodice-ripper heroine meets a cold, unattainable woman.
explanation.walkthrough: A bodice-ripper is a steamy historical romance; here the bodice itself is torn up.
explanation.definitionFit: Icebound means locked in by ice and so unreachable, literally frozen and inaccessible.

clue.text: Nothing of much substance In Elizabeth, ERII

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the run straddling the end of the name and the regnal cipher

explanation.surface: A sly dig that there is little of substance to Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.walkthrough: ERII is the royal cipher of Elizabeth II; the answer runs across the join.
explanation.definitionFit: The ether is the thin upper air or an imagined insubstantial medium, hardly anything of substance.

clue.text: see 10ac.
Do a Murdoch-style investigation: "Date Wants Rough Tight Ride"

indicators.note: rough means crude and disordered, so the words after it are knocked into a new shape

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for date
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline about a lurid date, in the style of Murdoch's papers.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Murdoch's tabloids were notorious for scandal-raking, including the phone-hacking affair.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig the dirt is to hunt out scandalous information, the stock-in-trade of a scandal sheet.

clue.text: Practices of conflict politician overlapping America

indicators.note: overlapping things share space, so the two pieces are woven into each other rather than set end to end

blocks.note: a war is an armed conflict
a Member of Parliament
the United States

explanation.surface: The habits of a warmongering politician who tags along with America.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-letter pieces interleave, each letter of one alternating with the other, after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Warm-ups are preparatory exercises or practice sessions done before the main event.

clue.text: Test reveals "Not a boozer with endless diarrhoea"

indicators.note: without an end means the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a dry person drinks no alcohol
the runs is slang for diarrhoea

explanation.surface: A medical test shows a teetotaller suffering from relentless diarrhoea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless diarrhoea' looks like a symptom, but it is an instruction to trim the slang term.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry run is a rehearsal or trial carried out before the real thing.
